extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of drama and literary criticism (dramatists, critics, and advanced literature students)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for the structure and character of tragic drama (after Aristotle): requirements for unity, plot causality, length/magnitude, temporal/spatial treatment, chorus function, and the qualities of the tragic hero that produce catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude/length of a work
rubrics_metrics.description: A work is unfit for artistic representation if it is infinitely large or infinitesimally small; the whole must be of such dimensions that the memory or mind's eye can embrace and retain it. A play should be of a magnitude sufficient to allow room for the natural development of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/explanation: The Trojan War is 'too vast in its compass' to be grasped for epic treatment; the poet must choose a beginning and an end so that the action is complete in itself. Avoid selecting a beginning that drags in an interminable chain of antecedents or an end that leaves matters unresolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reference to outward/accidental stage conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject as inartistic any reference to outward and accidental conditions of stage representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should not let incidental practicalities of the stage intrude on the artistic integrity of the piece; focus on the law of beauty governing the work rather than stage artifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (primary dramatic unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only dramatic unity enjoined by Aristotle: the action must be directed to a single end, with all parts subordinated to that end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is manifested by causal connexion binding parts together and by the convergence of events and moral forces to a single decisive point; the supreme test of unity is the concentrated impression of meaning when the end reveals the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal sequence and necessity in plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisive change of fortune must come about through the causal sequence of events; 'middle' marks causal relations, not mere temporal succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action must evolve freely and fully; beginnings, middles, and ends are defined by causal relations (beginning: does not itself follow by causal necessity; middle: follows something as something else follows it; end: naturally follows something and has nothing following it). The causal chain inside the drama should be strict but must not be indefinitely extended outwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: No episodic succession without inward connexion
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'epeisodic' plots in which scenes follow one another without inward connexion (a succession of stirring scenes does not make a tragedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: Euripides often substitutes pathetic effects, striking situations, and rapid contrasts for an articulated whole. Each scene must be inwardly connected to the plot's causal tissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denouement must arise from the plot itself (no Deus ex Machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unravelling or denouement must 'arise out of the plot itself,' not by recourse to Deus ex Machina or accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/anti-pattern: 'What did she die of?' 'Of what? of the fifth act'—i.e., an episodic fifth act or accidental ending undermines art. The need to avoid such devices is emphasised by theatrical history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic unity of parts (vital union, not mechanical piecing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure should be organic: a vital union of parts, not merely mechanical piecing together of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's recurring idea of parts 'suited to the whole' means parts must be inextricably interwoven (thoughts, emotions, will, and external events). Lowell: each scene should lead logically to something that follows and contribute impulse toward catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct selection of beginning, middle, and end
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning, middle, and end must be chosen so the action is complete: the beginning should not require endless antecedents; the middle must be causally connected to what goes before and after; the end should conclude the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet must avoid open-ended retrograde movement; choose a definite point to begin and end. The 'beginning' should be a relative beginning (follows other things in time but not as necessary consequence) so that the tragedy remains within the sphere of freedom and focused action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for complication and denouement relating to beginning/middle/end
rubrics_metrics.description: Complication (group of events before the decisive turn) and denouement (group of events after) structure the plot; the beginning ideally coincides with the beginning of the complication but may include pre-supposed external incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek practice often begins near the climax; ancient tragedies often resemble concluding acts of a larger action. The poet may admit incidents external to the action proper if they are presupposed and affect development (e.g., Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of recognition (anagnorisis) and reversal (peripeteia) when integral
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy may use surprises of Recognition and Reversal to intensify emotion, but these must be woven into the tissue of the plot and be the inevitable consequences of preceding events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices heighten tragic emotions when they are discovered, in light of the event, to be necessary consequences rather than arbitrary shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity (single end) revealed by convergent action
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole series of events and moral forces must be directed to a single end, with the action converging on a definite point and the thread of purpose becoming more marked as it advances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All minor effects should be subordinated to the sense of an ever-growing unity; in the end the meaning of the whole is discerned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate treatment of time (Unity of Time as a secondary rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general practice in Greek tragedy, the imaginary time of the dramatic action is limited, as far as possible, to a single revolution of the sun (roughly a day), but this is a prevailing usage rather than a strict rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars debate whether Aristotle meant 12 or 24 hours; practice allowed exceptions (e.g., The Trachiniae, Supplices, Agamemnon). Aristotle prefers unity of action; Unity of Time is secondary and may be relaxed using probability/verisimilitude if strict coincidence with representation isn't possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate treatment of place (Unity of Place as derivative/contingent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Place was generally observed in Greek drama (and later deduced by critics) but is not explicitly enjoined in the Poetics and should be tested against Unity of Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing scene/place can disturb unity; French dramatists derived strict place-unity from the ancients and imposed constraints (e.g., no scene shifts in same act, keep action within one town). The rule is derivative: if unity of action is preserved, time/place concerns are secondary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as structural bond and temporal/idealising function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus forms an ideal bond of union between separate parts and its choral odes can suspend outward action and idealise the interval of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral odes free the poet from strict temporal constraints—the interval covered by a choral ode 'is one whose value is just what the poet chooses to make it.' This allows flexibility in dramatizing time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between epic and dramatic form
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic can admit many episodes, retarding incidents, and simultaneous or collateral events (it is manifold and expansive); drama is more compact, concentrated, and presses forward to a single controlling end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences for practice: epic allows slower development and multiple tragic plots; drama requires concentrated sequence and moral inevitability—incidents should not be 'incidents and nothing more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid subordinating unity of action to time/place formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let minor unities (time/place) override the higher law of Unity of Action; enforcing strict time/place rules can compress action and violate inner consistency of character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical caution: French dramatists sometimes compressed events into 12-24 hours or avoided scene changes, harming character development and natural action. The higher principle is that unity of action must control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of probability/verisimilitude when necessity cannot be observed
rubrics_metrics.description: If strict equivalence between time of action and time of representation cannot be achieved, the poet may rely on probability (verisimilitude) to preserve plausibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle 'supplied the defect of necessity by probability' — allow the audience's imagination to accept plausible compressions or accelerations of time/place when necessary for art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of tragedy: produce katharsis (pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary function of tragedy is to produce the katharsis of pity and fear: pity for one who, though not wholly innocent, suffers beyond deserts; fear because the sufferer is of a nature like ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot must be capable of giving full satisfaction to these emotions; the tragic effect depends on both character and catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required in the tragic hero (neither eminently good nor wholly bad)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic hero should be such that pity and fear are aroused: an eminently good man meeting adverse fortune excites shock or repulsion rather than pity/fear; a bad man who prospers produces no pity or fear and fails to satisfy a sense of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic character must be intermediate—recognisable likeness to ourselves, suffering beyond deserts but not wholly innocent. Certain character types and forms of catastrophe are thereby excluded as failing to produce tragic effect.
